senses: The Hawaiian apostrophe-like letter (ʻ ) used to indicate the glottal stop consonant.
ety: Borrowed from Hawaiian ʻokina (“cutting off, separation”).

senses: A gelatinous mass of frogs' eggs, laid in ponds and ditches.
ety: From frog + spawn.

senses: table soccer (US), table football (UK)
ety: From German Fußball, itself a calque of English football.

senses: Any of several moths or caterpillars of the subfamily Thaumetopoeinae
ety: From procession + -ary.

senses: Corpselike; hinting of death; imitating a cadaver.
ety: From Latin cadāverōsus; compare Middle English cadaverous (“gangrenous, mortified”).
examples: Some approached pure blanching; some had a bluish pallor; some worn by the older characters (which had possibly lain by folded for many a year) inclined to a cadaverous tint, and to a Georgian style.

senses: One who strums a stringed musical instrument.
ety: From strum + -er.

senses: Somebody who quibbles.
ety: From quibble + -er.

senses: Curved in two directions, like the letter "S", or the Greek ς (sigma); having a serpentine shape.
Resembling a cat; feline.
Nimble, quick, graceful.
Slow, deliberate, quiet and stealthy.
ety: From cat + -like.

senses: Forming part of a ligament.
ety: From ligament + -ous.

senses: A rich stew originating in southwest France containing beans and meat.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French cassoulet, from Occitan caçolet.
examples: He’d made cassoulet, rich with pork and duck and lamb, glistening with oil and so delicious and sinful that everyone in the room let out audible sighs after their first bites.

senses: The status of being an alien; origin from elsewhere.
ety: From alien + -age.

senses: Synonym of jet bridge: an elevated corridor connecting an airport to a plane.
ety: From the trademarked Jetway, a common American manufacturer of jet bridges, from jet + way.

senses: In the shape of a pine cone.
ety: From French pinéal, from Middle French, from Latin pīnea (“pine cone, pine nut”), from pīneus (“of the pine”).

senses: Made to resemble pearl
ety: From pearl + -ize + -d.
examples: The models’ insolent pout was enhanced by a pearlized mouth.

senses: Dried and salted codfish.
ety: From Italian baccalà. Doublet of bacalhau and bacalao.

senses: One who gives details of something.
One who details (cleans cars).
ety: From detail + -er.

senses: A Japanese alcoholic beverage, most commonly distilled from barley, sweet potato or rice. Typically it is 25% alcohol by volume, making it weaker than whisky, but stronger than wine and sake.
ety: From Japanese 焼(しょう)酎(ちゅう) (shōchū), from Middle Chinese 燒酒 (syew tsjuw^X), from 燒 /烧 (shāo, “burn; flammable”) + 酒 (jiǔ, “alcohol”). Compare Mandarin 烧酒 (shāojiǔ), and Korean 소주 (soju). Doublet of shaojiu and soju.

senses: A baked case of dough with a sweet or savoury filling, popular in Eastern Europe.
ety: Borrowed from Russian пиро́г (piróg). Doublet of pierog/pieróg. For the plurals ending in n, see Yiddish פּיראָג (pirog).

senses: At once; immediately.
ety: From Hindi तत्काल (tatkāl, “on the spot”), from Sanskrit तत्कालीनं (tatkālīnaṃ, “for the present”), from तत् (tat, “that”) + कालीन (kālīna, “belonging to a particular time”).

senses: An espresso drink made with less hot water than normal.
ety: Borrowed from Italian ristretto (“concentrated”). Doublet of restrict.
examples: Formerly used only in Italy and Seattle, it includes such tongue activators as latte, lungo, cappuccino, ristretto, macchiato, mochaccino and Americano.

With eight pre-set beverage buttons all your favorite hot drinks are just one push away: cappuccino, latte, one or two cups of ristretto, espresso, large cups of crema coffee, even hot chocolate and tea.

senses: Exaggerated or caricatured, in the manner of a cartoon.
ety: From cartoon + -ish. Piecewise doublet of cartoonesque.
examples: She was grinning a big, cartoonish grin.

His requirement for compliments, flattery, adoration and awards is so continual and extreme that it is of cartoonish proportions, with all the garishness that characterizes the most exaggerated satire.

senses: The proprietor, manager, or operator of a small store.
ety: From shop + -man.

senses: Within a nucleus.
ety: From intra- + nuclear.

senses: A thing or person of no worth or value; nil.
Not any quantity of number; zero; the score of no points in a game.
The figure or character representing, or having the shape of, zero.
ety: From Middle English nought, noght, noȝt, from Old English nōwiht, nāwiht, which in turn comes from ne-ā-wiht, which was a phrase used as an emphatic "no", meaning "not anything". Equivalent to ne + ought or ne + a + wight. Doublet of naught and not.

senses: Able to be chemically or biologically degraded.
Having a complementary qubit channel and some third noise channel, such that adding the noise to the original channel replicates the complementary channel.
ety: From degrade + -able.

senses: A male roe deer.
ety: From Middle English roobukke; equivalent to roe + buck (“male deer”). Doublet of rhebok.

senses: A machine that bundles.
An employee who bundles things together, such as boards for trimming and stacking.
A political fundraiser.
ety: From bundle + -er.

senses: Tending to stutter.
ety: From stutter + -y.
examples: A buggier, stutterier, glitchier game I have never seen.
Moving on to the Samsung Daily screen, this is still by far the laggiest, stutteriest part of the entire software.

For 27.636 GB of your Switch's file space, you can play the choppiest and stutteriest mess of a version of Arkham Knight, a game that lets you traverse an open world city, like many other Switch games and ports.

senses: A bedroom or private apartments, especially for a woman in a medieval castle.
A shady, leafy shelter or recess in a garden or woods.
ety: From Middle English bour, from Old English būr, from Proto-West Germanic *būr, from Proto-Germanic *būrą (“room, abode”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Búur (“storage room, utility room; cage”), German Bauer (“birdcage”), Old Norse búr (“cage”) (Danish bur, Norwegian Bokmål bur, Swedish bur).
examples: Give me my lute in bed now as I lie, / And lock the doors of mine unlucky bower.

Rosa refused to return to the lair of the raper, but was induced to give Tudy what his mother described as ‘his last bit of happiness’ in a bower hastily got ready at Montrose, the La Plante mansion on Greenock Heights.

That night Tarzan built a snug little bower high among the swaying branches of a giant tree, and there the tired girl slept, while in a crotch beneath her the ape-man curled, ready, even in sleep, to protect her.

senses: A televised fundraising event encouraging viewers to make donations via telephone.
ety: A blend of telephone + marathon.

senses: A noticeable shift in society or culture in response to the activities or tastes of younger members of the culture.
ety: From youth + quake, by analogy with earthquake. Coined by American magazine editor Diana Vreeland in 1965.
examples: The trend was partly a manifestation of the Silicon Valley youthquake that was powering the dot-com economy.

senses: The game of rock paper scissors.
ety: From Japanese じゃんけん (janken).

senses: The act of motorizing something.
ety: From motorize + -ation.

senses: A Rastafarian person.
ety: Abbreviation of dreadlocks. Sense of “Rastafarian person” by synecdoche.

senses: The perch; any of various marine and freshwater fish resembling the perch.
ety: From Middle English bars, from Old English bærs (“a fish, perch”), from Proto-West Germanic *bars, from Proto-Germanic *barsaz (“perch”, literally “prickly”). Cognate with Dutch baars (“perch, bass”), German Barsch (“perch”). More at bass (“fish”).

senses: The act of bending a joint, especially a bone joint; the counteraction of extension.
The state of being bent or flexed.
Deviation from straightness.
ety: Borrowed from Latin flexiō, from flectō (“to bend, curve”) + -tiō, possibly via French. By surface analysis, flex + -ion.

senses: To see into; to observe acutely.
To have or gain insight into; to empathise with or come to fully understand one's point of view.
ety: From in- + see, or taken as a back-formation of inseeing, itself a loan-translation / calque of German Einsehen (“recognition, observation”). Compare Old English onsēon (“to look on, observe, regard, take notice of”). More at insight.
examples: First, moving from his internal region outwards to other internal regions, the speaker insees the "tear inside the stone."

This process of intuitional knowledge is strikingly analogous to the process of inseeing (Einsehen) Rilke described in his letters. I love inseeing. Can you imagine with me how glorious it is to insee...

senses: Lack or absence of fun; funlessness.
ety: From un- + fun.

senses: A restoration after decay or dilapidation; a renewal; a repair.
ety: From Latin instauratio: compare French instauration.
